questions.question: What does Cantor's diagonal argument show about $\mathbb{N}$ and $[0,1]$?
options: $[0,1]$ has strictly smaller cardinality than $\mathbb{R}$
There is no surjection from $[0,1]$ onto $\mathbb{N}$
There is no bijection between $\mathbb{N}$ and $[0,1]$
There is no injection from $\mathbb{N}$ into $[0,1]$

questions.question: In the diagonal argument, why is the newly constructed sequence not equal to the $i$th listed sequence?
options: It differs from that sequence in its first digit
It is chosen to differ from that sequence in every digit
It is chosen to differ from that sequence in the $i$th digit
It is a finite sequence, while the listed ones are infinite

questions.question: If the diagonal digits of a binary list begin $0,1,1,0$, what could the first four digits of the flipped diagonal sequence be?
What does the diagonal argument say about a claimed list $s_1,s_2,s_3,\ldots$ of all binary expansions in $[0,1]$?
options: The list must contain some binary expansion twice
The list is complete once every rational number appears on it
A binary expansion can be constructed that is not on the list
The missing expansion can be added, making the list complete

questions.question: If $s^*$ differs from every row in a proposed enumeration of $[0,1]$, what property of the enumeration fails?
options: Surjectivity onto all represented numbers
Well-definedness of the map from $n$ to row $s_n$
Injectivity of the labelling $n\mapsto s_n$ of rows
Countability of the index set $\mathbb{N}$ of rows

questions.question: Why is it not enough for the diagonal sequence to differ only from the first few rows?
options: Every later row is automatically different from it somewhere
The first few rows determine all the later rows of the claimed list
It must differ from each row in several digits, not one
To refute a complete list, it must differ from every listed row

questions.question: What assumption is contradicted in the diagonal argument?
options: That every number in $[0,1]$ has a binary expansion.
That $[0,1]$ contains infinitely many numbers.
That the list of expansions contains no repeated rows.
That the interval can be listed by natural numbers.

questions.question: What larger cardinality conclusion is supported by the diagonal argument?
options: The rational numbers have strictly larger cardinality than the natural numbers
No set has strictly larger cardinality than the real numbers
Every infinite subset of the reals has larger cardinality than the naturals
The real numbers have strictly larger cardinality than the natural numbers

questions.question: In the decimal version, each new digit differs from the diagonal digit and, from some point on, is taken from $\{1,2\}$, so the new expansion never ends in repeating $0$s or $9$s. Why is this precaution needed?
options: A new expansion could still name a listed number, since $0.1999\ldots=0.2000\ldots$
With $0$ or $9$ the new expansion could coincide digit for digit with a listed row
With $0$ or $9$ the new number could fall outside the interval $[0,1]$
Digits $1$ and $2$ make the new number larger than every listed number

questions.question: The rational numbers in $[0,1]$ can be listed as $q_1,q_2,q_3,\ldots$. Write each $q_i$ as a decimal expansion and build $x\in[0,1]$ whose $i$th digit is $1$ or $2$ and differs from the $i$th digit of $q_i$, so that $x\ne q_i$ for every $i$. Why does this not show that the rational numbers in $[0,1]$ are uncountable?
options: It does show it: the same construction proves that the rationals in $[0,1]$ are uncountable
The number $x$ is always one of the $q_i$, because the rationals are dense in $[0,1]$
The number $x$ need not be rational, so its absence from the list is no contradiction
The digits of $x$ repeat because those of each $q_i$ do, so $x$ is rational and on the list
